Large instrumental ensemble typical of [[Classical music|classical music]] or jazz, combining instruments from different families. A full orchestra has four main sections: strings ([[Violin|violin]], viola, [[Cello|cello]], double bass); woodwinds (flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon, and sometimes piccolo, cor anglais, bass clarinet, contrabassoon, and saxophone); brass (French horn, trumpet, trombone, tuba, and sometimes cornet and euphonium); and percussion (timpani, snare drum, bass drum, cymbals, triangle, tambourine, tam-tam, and mallet instruments). The [[Harp|harp]] is fairly regularly included in modern orchestras, especially for Romantic music. Keyboard instruments such as piano, harpsichord, pipe organ, and celesta may form a fifth section or appear as soloists.

A full-size Western orchestra may be called a symphony or philharmonic orchestra (from Greek phil-, "loving", and "harmony"). It numbers from seventy to over one hundred musicians, depending on the work and venue; a chamber orchestra has no more than around fifty. Orchestras specializing in [[Baroque music|Baroque]] repertoire, such as that of Bach and Handel, or in Haydn and Mozart, tend to be smaller than those playing Romantic works. The orchestra grew through the 18th and 19th centuries, peaking with as many as 120 players in works by [[Richard Wagner|Wagner]] and later [[Gustav Mahler|Mahler]]. The standard complement of paired winds and brass is generally attributed to the forces called for by [[Ludwig van Beethoven|Beethoven]].

A conductor, usually using a baton, unifies the orchestra, sets the tempo, shapes the sound, and leads rehearsals. The concertmaster, principal of the first violins, also leads the musicians. Orchestras play symphonies, overtures, concertos, and accompaniment for opera, ballet, and some musical theatre. Amateur orchestras include youth and community groups. The word derives from the Greek *orchestra*, the area in front of the stage in ancient Greek theatre reserved for the chorus.

Subdiscipline of chemistry concerned with the structure, properties, and reactions of organic compounds and organic materials, those containing [[Carbon|carbon]] atoms. It includes determining structural formulas, analyzing physical and chemical properties, evaluating reactivity, and the synthesis of natural products, drugs, and polymers.

The field covers [[Hydrocarbon|hydrocarbons]] (compounds of only carbon and hydrogen) and compounds that also contain oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, phosphorus, and the halogens. Carbon's valence of four, with single, double, and triple bonds and delocalized electrons, makes organic compounds structurally diverse. They form the basis of all known life and underlie pharmaceuticals, petrochemicals, agrichemicals, lubricants, solvents, plastics, fuels, and explosives. The field overlaps [[Organometallic chemistry|organometallic chemistry]], [[Biochemistry|biochemistry]], medicinal chemistry, polymer chemistry, and materials science.

Before the 18th century, chemists generally believed that compounds from living organisms held a "vital force" (vitalism). Around 1816 Michel Chevreul showed that fats could be chemically changed into new compounds. In 1828 [[Friedrich Wöhler|Friedrich Wöhler]] produced urea from potassium cyanate and ammonium sulfate, a synthesis now generally accepted as disproving vitalism, though Wöhler himself was cautious. [[Justus von Liebig|Justus von Liebig]] is considered one of the field's principal founders. In 1856 William Henry Perkin accidentally produced the dye known as Perkin's mauve, and in 1858 Friedrich August Kekulé and Archibald Scott Couper independently developed the concept of chemical structure.

Bayer first manufactured [[Aspirin|aspirin]] in the last decade of the 19th century. By 1910 Paul Ehrlich's group was developing the arsenic-based Salvarsan against syphilis, beginning chemotherapy. Natural indigo production fell from 19,000 tons in 1897 to 1,000 tons by 1914 thanks to Adolf von Baeyer's synthetic methods. Total synthesis later reached molecules as complex as vitamin B12.

Living thing that functions as an individual, a definition that raises more problems than it solves because the concept of an individual is itself difficult. Several criteria have been proposed, few widely accepted. The most common is autonomous reproduction, growth, and [[Metabolism|metabolism]], which would exclude [[Virus|viruses]]: they cannot reproduce, grow, or metabolize on their own, and cannot synthesize the organic compounds of which they are formed.

The English term appeared in the 1660s, from the Ancient Greek *organismos*, related to *organon* ("instrument, implement, tool"). In his 1790 *Critique of Judgment*, [[Immanuel Kant]] defined an organism as "both an organized and a self-organizing being". Other proposed criteria include noncompartmentability, stated by [[Richard Dawkins]] as "the quality of being sufficiently heterogeneous in form to be rendered non-functional if cut in half" (though many organisms can be cut into pieces that regrow); individuality; an immune response; "anti-entropy", the ability to maintain order, first proposed by [[Erwin Schrödinger]]; the capacity to maintain information content, as in [[Claude Shannon]]'s information theory; and having cells. Some scientists consider the concept inadequate for biology.

Colonial organisms are problematic cases. A colony of eusocial insects shows adaptive organization and germ-soma specialization, and a siphonophore is composed of organism-like zooids. David Queller and Joan Strassmann propose cooperation as the defining trait, which would count a [[Lichen|lichen]], a partnership of fungi with algae or cyanobacteria, and the permanent sexual partnership of an [[Anglerfish|anglerfish]] as organisms. Others argue that autonomy, genetic homogeneity, and genetic uniqueness should be examined separately.

Unicellular organisms (protists, bacteria, archaea) consist of a single cell; multicellular organisms (animals, plants, fungi, algae) of many. Organisms are commonly classified into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya.

State (c. 1299–1922) that spanned much of Southeastern Europe, West Asia, and North Africa, centred in modern-day Turkey. It also controlled parts of southeastern Central Europe between the early 16th and early 18th centuries.

The empire emerged from a principality founded in northwestern Anatolia in c. 1299 by the Turkoman tribal leader [[Osman I]]. His successors conquered much of Anatolia and expanded into the Balkans by the mid-14th century. [[Mehmed II]] ended the Byzantine Empire with the conquest of [[Constantinople]] in 1453, and further conquests by [[Selim I]] led the sultans to adopt the title of caliph. Ruling diverse peoples, the empire granted its confessional communities, or millets, autonomy to manage their own affairs under Islamic law. Under [[Suleiman the Magnificent]] in the 16th century it became a global power.

The empire reached its greatest extent in 1683, on the eve of the second Siege of Vienna. Modern academic consensus holds that decline began after that defeat, though a flexible economy, society, and military persisted into much of the 18th century. The 1876 revolution attempted constitutional monarchy before a reversion to absolute monarchy under [[Abdul Hamid II]]. The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 restored constitutional rule, but after the Balkan Wars the Committee of Union and Progress established a dictatorship in 1913.

The empire joined [[World War I]] on the side of the Central Powers and engaged in genocide against Armenians, Assyrians, and Greeks. The Allies occupied and partitioned it afterward. The Turkish War of Independence, led by [[Mustafa Kemal Atatürk]], ended the sultanate in 1922; the Grand National Assembly of Turkey abolished it on November 1, 1922.

Expanse beyond Earth's atmosphere and between celestial bodies. It is a near-perfect [[Vacuum|vacuum]] of predominantly hydrogen and helium plasma, permeated by electromagnetic radiation, cosmic rays, neutrinos, magnetic fields, and dust. Its baseline temperature, set by background radiation from the [[Big Bang]], is 2.7 kelvins (−270 °C). The plasma between galaxies is thought to account for about half of the ordinary matter in the observable universe, at fewer than one hydrogen atom per cubic metre. Most of the remaining mass-energy is made up of unknown forms called [[Dark matter|dark matter]] and dark energy.

Space has no definite starting altitude. The [[Kármán line]], 100 km above sea level, is conventionally used as its start in space treaties and aerospace records. The Outer Space Treaty, in force since October 10, 1967, precludes claims of national sovereignty and permits all states to explore freely.

According to Big Bang theory, the universe was extremely hot and dense about 13.8 billion years ago and rapidly expanded. About 380,000 years later it had cooled enough for protons and electrons to combine into hydrogen. Remaining matter collapsed into stars and galaxies, leaving the deep vacuum now called outer space.

The term "outer space" was first applied in astronomy in 1845 by Alexander von Humboldt. Exploration began with high-altitude balloons, then rockets. The Soviet Union launched [[Sputnik 1]] on October 4, 1957, and [[Yuri Gagarin]] achieved crewed Earth orbit in 1961. Apollo 11 landed on the Moon in 1969, and the [[International Space Station]] has been continuously occupied since 2000. High cost limits human flight to low Earth orbit and the Moon, while uncrewed craft have reached all known planets. Vacuum, radiation, and microgravity, which causes muscle atrophy and bone loss, endanger humans.

Tool with a hollow chamber that exposes materials to a controlled hot environment. Ovens have been used since antiquity and differ by purpose and by how they generate heat. Most often they are used for [[Cooking|cooking]], usually baking and sometimes broiling. Ovens for ceramics and pottery are sometimes called kilns, metallurgical furnaces make metals, and glass furnaces make glass.

Some ovens burn fuel such as wood, coal, or natural gas; many use electricity. Electric ovens and furnaces use resistive heating, while microwave ovens expose materials to microwave radiation, which excites water molecules in food. Some ovens use forced convection, the movement of gases inside the chamber, to speed heating.

The earliest known ovens, in Central Europe, date to 29,000 BC: roasting and boiling pits inside yurts used to cook mammoth. In Ukraine from 20,000 BC, people used pits of hot coals covered in ashes. Clay ovens appeared in homes at [[Çatalhöyük]] by 6600 BC, in pre-dynastic Egypt c. 5000–4000 BC, and throughout [[Mesopotamia]] by 4000 BC, with examples at Ur, Nippur, and Eridu. By 3200 BC cultures of the [[Indus Valley Civilisation]] used ovens to cook food and make bricks. The tandır, a cylindrical oven that bakes unleavened flatbread stuck to its walls, was common in Anatolia and remains central to rural food culture there.

In the Middle Ages, Europeans used fireplaces with large cauldrons. Cast-iron stoves came into use in the early 1700s, and the coal oven was developed in the early 19th century. James Sharp patented one of the first gas stoves in 1826, and Gustaf Dalén invented the AGA cooker in 1922. Percy Spencer discovered microwave cooking in 1946, leading to the microwave oven.

Chemical element, symbol O, atomic number 8, a nonmetal of the chalcogen group in the [[Periodic table|periodic table]]. It is highly reactive and a potent oxidizing agent, readily forming oxides with most elements. It is the most abundant element in [[Earth's crust]], making up almost half of it, chiefly as water, carbon dioxide, iron oxides, and silicates, and the third most abundant in the universe after hydrogen and helium.

At standard temperature and pressure, two atoms bind covalently to form dioxygen (O₂), a colorless, odorless gas that is currently about 20.95% of Earth's atmosphere by molar fraction. The rarer allotrope [[Ozone|ozone]] (O₃) absorbs UVB and UVC radiation, forming a protective layer in the lower stratosphere, but at the surface it is a corrosive air pollutant. Oxygen is too reactive to remain free in air without continuous replenishment by [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]] in cyanobacteria, algae, and land plants.

Aerobic [[Respiration (physiology)|respiration]] extracts energy by reacting oxygen with organic molecules from food, releasing carbon dioxide. Proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and fats contain oxygen, as do shells, teeth, and bone, and most of the mass of living organisms is oxygen in water.

The modern concept developed over five centuries, and no one person discovered oxygen. Michael Sendivogius isolated the substance before 1604, calling it *cibus vitae* ("food of life"). John Mayow proposed in 1668 that part of the air is consumed in both respiration and [[Combustion|combustion]]. Carl Wilhelm Scheele in Uppsala (1773 or earlier) and [[Joseph Priestley]] in Wiltshire (1774) discovered it independently; Priestley called it "dephlogisticated air" and did not recognize it as an element. In 1777 [[Antoine Lavoisier]] first recognized it as a chemical element and correctly described its role in combustion.

Spanish painter, sculptor, printmaker, and ceramicist who spent most of his adult life in France. He co-founded the [[Cubism|Cubist]] movement, invented constructed sculpture, co-invented [[Collage|collage]], and produced about 50,000 artworks in a career of more than 76 years. Among his best-known works are the proto-Cubist [[Les Demoiselles d'Avignon|*Les Demoiselles d'Avignon*]] (1907) and the anti-war painting [[Guernica (Picasso)|*Guernica*]] (1937), a portrayal of the bombing of Guernica during the [[Spanish Civil War]].

Born in [[Málaga]], the first child of the painter José Ruiz y Blasco, he began formal training under his father at age seven. The family moved to A Coruña in 1891. After his seven-year-old sister Conchita died of diphtheria in 1895, they moved to [[Barcelona]], where Picasso, at 13, passed the entrance exam for the advanced class at the School of Fine Arts in a week. He settled in Paris in 1904.

His style changed repeatedly in the first decade of the 20th century. After 1906, the Fauvist work of the older artist [[Henri Matisse]] pushed him toward more radical styles and began a rivalry in which critics often paired the two as leaders of modern art. The commonly accepted periods of his work are the Blue Period (1901–1904), the Rose Period (1904–1906), the African-influenced Period (1907–1909), Analytic Cubism (1909–1912), and Synthetic Cubism (1912–1919). His work of the late 1910s and early 1920s is often neoclassical, and that of the mid-1920s shows traits of Surrealism. Later work combines earlier styles. He achieved great renown and fortune. Accounts of his relationships with partners such as Fernande Olivier, Olga Khokhlova, Marie-Thérèse Walter, Dora Maar, and Françoise Gilot describe them as domineering and emotionally abusive, prompting posthumous criticism of misogyny.

Largest and deepest of Earth's five oceanic divisions, stretching from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the [[Southern Ocean]] or, by some definitions, Antarctica in the south, and bounded by Asia and Australia in the west and the Americas in the east.

With an area of 165,250,000 sq km (defined with a southern Antarctic border), it covers about 46% of Earth's water surface and about 32% of the planet's total surface, more than all land combined. Circulation divides it into the North and South Pacific, which meet at the [[Equator|Equator]]; the [[International Date Line]] informally divides it into east and west. Mean depth is 4,000 m. [[Challenger Deep]], in the [[Mariana Trench]], is the deepest known point in the world at 10,928 m, and the Horizon Deep in the Tonga Trench, at 10,823 m, is the deepest point in the Southern Hemisphere. More than 25,000 islands rise above its surface, many of them the remains of volcanoes, and it is ringed by the [[Ring of Fire]], a belt of volcanoes and earthquake zones driven by subduction of the Pacific Plate.

In 1513 the Spanish explorer Vasco Núñez de Balboa sighted what he named the Mar del Sur. The current name was coined during the Spanish circumnavigation of 1520 by [[Ferdinand Magellan]], who found favorable winds and called it *Mar Pacífico* ("peaceful sea").

Modern humans first reached the western Pacific around 60,000 to 70,000 years ago, crossing at least 80 km of sea between Sundaland and Sahul to reach Australia. The later Neolithic expansion of the [[Austronesian peoples]], from Taiwan c. 3000–1500 BCE, brought outrigger and sailing technology to the first settlement of Remote Oceania, reaching the Marianas by 1500 BCE and Palau and Yap by 1000 BCE.

Visual art characterized by applying paint, pigment, color, or another medium to a solid surface. The medium is commonly applied with a brush, but palette knives, sponges, airbrushes, fingers, or dripping may also be used. The term describes both the act and the resulting work. Supports include walls, paper, canvas, wood, glass, lacquer, pottery, leaf, and copper, and paintings may incorporate sand, clay, plaster, gold leaf, or entire objects.

Painting brings together drawing, composition, gesture, narration, and abstraction. It may be naturalistic and representational, as in portraits, still life, and landscape, or abstract, narrative, symbolist, emotive, or political. A significant share of its history in both Eastern and Western art has been dominated by religious subjects, from mythological figures on pottery to Biblical scenes on the Sistine Chapel ceiling and the life of Buddha.

The oldest known paintings are more than 40,000–60,000 years old and occur in caves in Maros, Sulawesi, Indonesia. A study published in *Nature* on July 3, 2024, dated [[Cave painting|cave paintings]] at Leang Karampuang, showing human-like figures interacting with a pig and measuring 91 by 38 cm, to about 51,200 years ago, making them the oldest known. Western traditions favor [[Oil painting|oil]] and [[Watercolor painting|watercolor]], refined in 15th-century Europe, while ink long predominated in the East.

After the first photograph was produced in 1829, [[Photography|photography]] deprived painting of much of its role in recording the visible world. [[Impressionism]], Post-Impressionism, Fauvism, Expressionism, Cubism, and Dadaism then challenged the Renaissance view of the world. Twentieth-century abstraction, as in [[Piet Mondrian]]'s geometries and [[Jackson Pollock]]'s drip methods, favored form, color, and gesture. Color, made up of hue, saturation, and value, is the essence of painting; black signifies mourning in the West and white in the East.
